entry.evidence: Very little is known how basin-wide development and climate change would impact the Cambodian Mekong floodplain other than the Tonle Sap

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML full text (jats_text), with PDF for figures

steps.action: Authors review prior model projections of Mekong flow and flood change under climate change, hydropower and irrigation (Hoang 2016, 2019; Lauri 2012; Try 2020a; Triet 2020) as the expectations the study builds on.
steps.quote: hydropower development plans in the Mekong River basin are expected to increase dry season flows

steps.action: Authors name the gap (cumulative multi-driver impacts on the Cambodian Mekong floodplain outside the Tonle Sap) and set the aim of quantifying them at provincial level.
steps.quote: Very little is known how basin-wide development and climate change would impact the Cambodian Mekong floodplain other than the Tonle Sap

steps.action: Authors build a chained model setup: basin model IWRM-VMod drives 1D MIKE 11, whose outputs are boundary conditions for the 1 km 2D floodplain model IWRM-Sub.
steps.quote: We used a hydrological–floodplain model combination

steps.action: Basin-wide IWRM-VMod baseline and scenario runs are taken from the authors' earlier study rather than rerun.
steps.quote: We used the model runs, both baseline and scenarios, from Hoang et al. (2019).

steps.action: Authors compare CMIP5 and CMIP6 mean precipitation and temperature over the study area to check that the CMIP5 forcing is not outdated (Supplement Table S1).
steps.quote: an analysis of the differences between model collections shows consistent mean values

steps.action: Authors recalibrate the model chain for the 1971–2000 baseline against discharge and water level at four Cambodian stations.
steps.quote: advancing the predictive accuracy of the hydrology (recalibration), accounting for multiple calibration stations (four stations)

steps.action: Authors adopt the 12-scenario design from Hoang et al. (2019): pre-2000 baseline, hydropower, two irrigation levels, RCP4.5/8.5 from five GCMs, and combinations. They add a cited 43 cm sea-level offset and cited dam operation rules.
steps.quote: The scenario setup that we adopted for our study is the same as that described in Hoang et al. (2019).

steps.action: Authors validate IWRM-Sub against station discharge and water level (NSE, PBIAS, RSR, R2 against literature thresholds; Table 3) and against Landsat/SWMT flood extent (recall, precision, area ratio; Figure 3). Earlier validations of IWRM-VMod and MIKE 11 are cited.
steps.quote: a good model performance is obtained at all stations (both water discharge and water level)

steps.action: Authors attribute the about 29% non-overlap between simulated and observed flood extent partly to rivers and lakes being in the simulated but not the satellite extent, rather than revising the model.
steps.quote: Part of this discrepancy may be accounted for by the inclusion of rivers and lakes in the extent of the simulation

steps.action: Authors keep the model chain as adequate, stating that compounding of errors across the chain did not unduly affect results.
steps.quote: these results demonstrate that this has not unduly impacted our methodology

steps.action: Authors run all scenarios S1–S12 and compute percentage change in mean monthly discharge and water level at each station relative to the baseline.
steps.quote: Having run the model for each of the development scenarios (S1–S12; see Table 2)

steps.action: Authors compare scenario hydrographs with the baseline at Kampong Cham and Neak Loeung: hydropower raises dry-season and lowers wet-season flows, and climate change partly offsets this downstream.
steps.quote: All scenarios that contain an element of hydropower development follow the same pattern of increasing both water discharge and water level during the dry season

steps.action: Authors keep the claim that hydropower dominates the change in main-channel hydrology over irrigation and climate change.
steps.quote: planned hydropower developments will drastically alter the hydrology of the Mekong main channel

steps.action: Authors simulate baseline flood conditions: yearly flooded area of 7785–11 525 km2, mean 9370 km2.
steps.quote: Its mean annual value is estimated at 9370 km2, about 34 % of the whole study area.

steps.action: Authors compare year-to-year total flooded area (Figure 5) and spatial depth and duration changes (Figure 6) for each scenario against the baseline.
steps.quote: there is a clear pattern that emerges, once again showing the dominance of hydropower development in significantly reducing the yearly flooded area

steps.action: Authors keep the claims that flood extent falls by more than 20% under hydropower and that impacts are spatially heterogeneous, shifting flood impacts between areas.
steps.quote: all scenarios will cause heterogeneous impacts across the region that may effectively shift flood impacts from one area to another

steps.action: Authors compare flooded area, depth and duration change by province for 10 provinces; Svay Rieng is flagged as anomalous.
steps.quote: Kampong Chhnang and Kratie are least affected by the impacts of climate change, whilst Prey Veng and Takéo are most affected

steps.action: Authors compare their baseline performance metrics with those of earlier regional studies (Västilä 2010; Dang 2018; Fujii 2003; Try 2020a, b).
steps.quote: exceed existing studies within the same region (Västilä et al., 2010), with the exception of Dang et al. (2018)

steps.action: Authors state high confidence in their projections on the strength of baseline performance.
steps.quote: The relative success of our baseline simulations allows us to have a high degree of confidence in our future projections

steps.action: Authors set their projected trends against published studies and report agreement, both for flows and for flood conditions.
steps.quote: These general trends are in line with the majority of previous research in the region

steps.action: Authors propose untested explanations for provincial differences: Tonle Sap control of Kampong Chhnang, low elevation of Svay Rieng, and possible influence from the Vietnamese delta.
steps.quote: most likely because the flood regime is strongly controlled by the Tonle Sap Lake system

steps.action: Authors keep the headline claim: combined development lowers wet-season and raises dry-season flows and levels, partly counteracted by climate change, and the model setup performs well.
steps.quote: The combined development scenarios that we analysed exhibited the same pattern of decreasing hydrological conditions during the wet season

tree.answer: Future change in floodplain hydrology and flooding under development and climate change
No; future conditions are known only by model projection
Quantify cumulative multi-driver impacts at station and provincial level
No rival hypotheses; drivers are compared in isolation and in combination as scenarios
Scenarios differ: hydropower and climate change act in opposite directions in the wet season
Conditions set in silico by scenario forcing of the model chain
Model validated against four stations and satellite flood extent; CMIP6 forcing compared; no sensitivity runs
Kept: hydropower dominates and flood extent falls by about 20%
No review file supplied; two anonymous referees acknowledged

end.claim: By about 2050, combined hydropower, irrigation and climate-change scenarios alter Cambodian Mekong floodplain flows (early wet season down to about -30%, mid-dry season up to about +140%) and reduce total flood extent by around 20%. Hydropower dominates these changes.

decisive_move.sentence: Running the twelve scenarios through the recalibrated three-model chain and differencing against the 1971–2000 baseline produced every projected change; without it no claim exists.

gates.evidence: No hypothesis directed data acquisition. Scenario design and model runs were inherited (§2.2 ¶1, §2.4 ¶1). The model faced validation it could have failed against literature thresholds for NSE, PBIAS, RSR and R2 (§3.1 ¶2; Table 3), and against satellite flood extent (§3.1 ¶3). The projections themselves face no test. The performance thresholds (Benaman 2005; Setegn 2010) and the scenario set (Hoang 2019) were fixed before this analysis; nothing else was registered.

imports.item: 2D depth-averaged Navier–Stokes and St. Venant equations in IWRM-Sub
recall and precision indices for comparing simulated and observed flood extent

novelty_claims.quote: we used an innovative combination of three models
the present study is a novel contribution to the work being done to understand the potential for future changes
this research uses a novel setup of three different models

limits:
Sub-claims and their statuses: (1) the model setup performs well and could be reused elsewhere: capability_characterized (§5 ¶1). (2) Provincial explanations (Tonle Sap control, low elevation of Svay Rieng): hypotheses only, untested (§4.1 ¶5). (3) Hydropower dominance over other drivers: estimate within the scenario set (§3.2 ¶4).

Uncertainty: projections are reported as ensemble-driven percentage changes, with interannual spread only (Figure 5). Inference: the spread across individual GCMs, the effect of the fixed 43 cm sea-level offset, and the effect of model-chain parameters are not reported, so 'resolution' rests on interannual variability.

Validation: calibration and validation both use 1985–2000 station data, so the validation is not on held-out data (inference from §2.3 ¶2 and Table 3). Flood-extent recall and precision of 0.71 and 0.72 are explained away rather than investigated (§3.1 ¶3). The text says total area is underestimated by 0.1% while the ratio is 0.99; inference: these are inconsistent.

Traceability: the abstract's -30% and +140% figures are not stated in the results text and are presumably read off Figure 4.

Provenance: no review file was supplied, so revisions forced by the two referees cannot be coded. Much of the pipeline (basin runs, scenarios, MIKE 11 setup, dam rules) is inherited from the authors' earlier work.

Composition: none_fits because this is a scenario-projection study with no rivals, no new observation, and no frozen forecast scored later.

disagreements.target: Västilä et al. (2010); Dang et al. (2018); Fujii et al. (2003); Try et al. (2020a, b)
disagreements.support: Station NSE, PBIAS, RSR and R2 values are compared with reported metrics; the paper claims to exceed most multi-year studies while conceding that Dang (2018) and single-event Fujii (2003) score higher.
disagreements.quote: our continual analysis of annual flood patterns comprising a 30-year time horizon is comparable to, and often exceeds, other such multi-year analyses
